stem: Several months after an axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer, a client reports that the affected-side arm feels newly heavy and tight and appears mildly swollen. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Assess and compare both arms for swelling and other changes and promptly arrange evaluation for possible lymphedema.
options.B: Reassure the client that heaviness and tightness are expected after axillary surgery and require evaluation only if the swelling becomes severe.
options.C: Encourage immediate heavy resistance exercise with the affected arm before any assessment is completed.
options.D: Assume the symptoms prove lymphedema and begin tight compression wrapping without evaluation or fitting by the healthcare team.

rationale: A is correct. NCI states that lymph-node removal increases lymphedema risk after breast-cancer treatment and advises clients to report even slight changes such as a heavy, full, or tight feeling and swelling. When an arm is affected, evaluation includes examination and comparison with the other limb; additional testing may be used to evaluate causes of swelling. B is incorrect because early symptoms should be reported rather than dismissed until severe. C is incorrect because exercise should be individualized and safe; new symptoms warrant assessment before an unsupervised heavy program. D is incorrect because symptoms do not establish the diagnosis by themselves and compression garments or wraps should be appropriately selected and taught by the healthcare team or certified lymphedema therapist.
educational_objective: Recognize early upper-extremity lymphedema symptoms after axillary lymph-node dissection and prioritize prompt assessment and comparison of the affected limb rather than delaying evaluation or starting unassessed treatment.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Lymphedema and Cancer; Lymphedema (PDQ®) — Health Professional Version
source_version_date: Lymphedema and Cancer updated 2024-03-06; current NCI PDQ accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: Lymphedema and Cancer — 'What causes lymphedema?' breast-cancer subsection; 'What are symptoms of lymphedema?' lines describing heavy/full/tight feeling and limb swelling; 'How is lymphedema diagnosed?' arm/leg comparison and diagnostic testing; 'How is lymphedema treated?' compression and CLT guidance; 'Can I prevent lymphedema?' exercise guidance.
source_claim_supported: Axillary lymph-node removal increases lymphedema risk; early heaviness, tightness and swelling should be reported and assessed; limb comparison is part of evaluation; exercise and compression should be individualized and appropriately supervised.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — recognize treatment-related complications, perform focused assessments, recognize changes in client condition, and intervene as needed.
correction_summary: Completely removed the source item's blanket post-axillary-dissection prohibition on blood pressure, injections and constriction. Current NCI specifically frames contralateral BP/blood-draw advice for established lymphedema, not as a universal evidence-based rule for every merely at-risk arm. The final item instead tests directly supported early symptom recognition and assessment.
audit_findings: Current NCI guidance does not support presenting all BP measurements/injections on an at-risk post-ALND arm as a universal prohibition; the source construct was therefore rebuilt.
The final stem uses NCI-listed early findings: new heaviness, tightness, and swelling after lymph-node removal.
NCI directly supports prompt reporting, examination, and comparison of limb size; diagnostic testing may be required for other causes of swelling.
No diagnosis is assumed and no compression or exercise prescription is started without appropriate assessment.
Independent adversarial review found no outdated blanket precaution, second answer, cueing, unsupported threshold, locator defect, or unresolved conflict.
